title: Chapter 11 Drill: Neuro-ophthalmology, Neuro-otology, Trauma, Neuro-oncology, and Toxic-Metabolic Disease

items.stem: A 50-year-old man has progressive right-sided hearing loss and tinnitus over a year. Weber testing lateralizes to the left, and the right corneal reflex is reduced. Magnetic resonance imaging is most likely to show which finding?
options: Enhancing mass in the right cerebellopontine angle
Enlargement of the right endolymphatic sac only
Bilateral symmetric periventricular white matter lesions
items.explanation: Unilateral sensorineural hearing loss with a Weber test that lateralizes away from the affected ear and trigeminal involvement indicates a retrocochlear lesion. Vestibular schwannoma enlarging into the cerebellopontine angle can reduce the corneal reflex by compressing the fifth nerve. A lacune would not cause isolated hearing loss, and bilateral white matter lesions would not explain unilateral deficits.

items.stem: A family of four is found with headache, nausea, and confusion after using a portable generator in a closed garage during winter. Pulse oximetry reads 99 percent. What is the best immediate treatment?
items.explanation: Carbon monoxide binds hemoglobin with greater affinity than oxygen, and standard pulse oximetry cannot tell carboxyhemoglobin from oxyhemoglobin, giving a falsely normal reading. High-flow oxygen shortens the carboxyhemoglobin half-life, and hyperbaric treatment is considered with syncope, neurologic deficits, or high levels. Room air is too slow. Methylene blue treats methemoglobinemia, and hydroxocobalamin treats cyanide poisoning.

items.stem: A 44-year-old man reports bumping into objects on his left side. Visual field testing shows a left homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing, and the pupillary light reflexes are normal. Where is the lesion most likely located?
items.explanation: A homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing and normal pupillary reflexes localizes to the occipital cortex, where the dual blood supply of the occipital pole spares central vision. An optic tract lesion usually produces an incongruous defect with an afferent pupillary defect in the contralateral eye. A chiasmal lesion causes bitemporal loss, and an optic nerve lesion causes monocular loss.

items.stem: A 62-year-old vegan man has numb, tingling feet, loss of vibration and position sense, and a spastic gait with brisk knee jerks. Hemoglobin is 10.5 g/dL with a mean corpuscular volume of 112 fL. Which condition explains the findings?
items.explanation: Posterior and lateral column involvement with a peripheral neuropathy and macrocytic anemia is classic for vitamin B12 deficiency. Elevated methylmalonic acid and homocysteine support the diagnosis. Tabes dorsalis shares dorsal column loss but has lightning pains and Argyll Robertson pupils, and Friedreich ataxia begins in youth. Copper deficiency can look identical but needs a copper level to separate it.

items.stem: A 29-year-old man with a chronic cervical cord injury develops a pounding headache, flushing above the lesion, and blood pressure of 210/110 mm Hg. What is the first step in management?
options: Give intravenous methylprednisolone as an urgent bolus
Sit upright and search for a noxious trigger
Perform a diagnostic lumbar puncture right now
Lay him flat and start a rapid fluid bolus
items.explanation: Autonomic dysreflexia occurs in lesions above T6 when a stimulus such as a distended bladder or bowel produces uninhibited sympathetic reflex activity. Management is to sit the patient up, loosen constrictive clothing, relieve the trigger, and then treat persistent hypertension with a short acting agent. Lying flat worsens hypertension, and steroids and lumbar puncture are not indicated.

items.stem: A 46-year-old woman presents with fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, carpal tunnel symptoms, and delayed relaxation of ankle reflexes. Creatine kinase is mildly elevated. Which condition is the most likely cause?
items.explanation: Delayed relaxation phase of tendon reflexes, myopathy with raised creatine kinase, and entrapment neuropathy such as carpal tunnel syndrome suggest hypothyroidism. Cushing syndrome gives proximal weakness without a raised enzyme level, and hyperparathyroidism produces weakness with hypercalcemia. Acromegaly also causes carpal tunnel syndrome but with different systemic features and brisk reflexes. Treatment with levothyroxine usually reverses the neuromuscular findings.

items.stem: A 24-year-old woman has acute abdominal pain, constipation, tachycardia, and a rapidly ascending motor neuropathy with hyponatremia after starting a new antiseizure drug. Her urine darkens on standing. What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Increased dose of the new antiseizure drug
items.explanation: Abdominal pain, autonomic instability, hyponatremia, a motor neuropathy, and darkening urine suggest acute intermittent porphyria, which can be triggered by cytochrome inducing drugs. Hemin suppresses hepatic production of porphyrin precursors, and carbohydrate loading helps in mild attacks. Immunoglobulin treats Guillain-Barre syndrome, which does not explain the abdominal pain and urine. Steroids and more of the trigger drug would worsen the attack.

items.stem: A 29-year-old man develops fever, headache, and confusion on a week of high-dose methotrexate, and nothing infectious is found. Which neurotoxic effect is most characteristic of intrathecal or high-dose systemic methotrexate?
items.explanation: Methotrexate, especially intrathecal or high-dose with cranial radiation, causes chemical meningitis, encephalopathy, and a leukoencephalopathy with white matter T2 signal change. Peripheral neuropathy with autonomic failure is typical of vincristine, ototoxicity of cisplatin, and optic neuropathy is not the usual methotrexate effect. Leucovorin rescue limits systemic toxicity but does not protect against intrathecal injury. Risk rises with cranial radiation and high cumulative doses.

items.stem: A 59-year-old woman with lung cancer has a single 2-cm brain metastasis in the right cerebellum with no other metastases and controlled systemic disease. Which treatment is most appropriate for a single small lesion?
items.explanation: For a limited number of small brain metastases in a patient with controlled systemic disease, stereotactic radiosurgery or resection gives local control with less cognitive toxicity than whole brain radiation. Whole brain radiation alone is reserved for many lesions. Systemic chemotherapy rarely controls brain lesions quickly, and leaving a posterior fossa lesion untreated risks hydrocephalus.

items.stem: A 40-year-old man with chronic fat malabsorption from cystic fibrosis develops ataxia, areflexia, and loss of proprioception. Retinal examination shows early pigmentary changes. Which deficiency is most likely?
items.explanation: Fat soluble vitamin E deficiency from malabsorption causes a spinocerebellar syndrome resembling Friedreich ataxia, with areflexia, proprioceptive loss, and retinopathy. Thiamine deficiency produces Wernicke syndrome or beriberi, and niacin deficiency causes pellagra with dermatitis, diarrhea, and dementia. Vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy with bleeding and perifollicular hemorrhage. Treatment is high-dose vitamin E supplementation, and the findings can be partly reversible if started early.

items.stem: A 42-year-old man with known adrenal insufficiency stops his glucocorticoid replacement and develops lethargy, hypotension, hyponatremia, and hyperkalemia. What is the correct immediate treatment?
options: Fluid restriction with oral salt tablets
items.explanation: Adrenal crisis presents with shock, altered mental state, hyponatremia, and hyperkalemia, and needs immediate hydrocortisone plus volume resuscitation. Fluid restriction would worsen hypotension. Potassium is already high, so replacement is dangerous, and hypertonic saline risks overly fast sodium correction when volume repletion alone will correct the sodium. Glucocorticoid replacement must never be delayed to confirm the diagnosis with testing.

items.stem: A 71-year-old woman with macular degeneration reports seeing detailed images of children and animals in the room. She knows they are not real and has no cognitive decline or other psychiatric symptoms. What is the diagnosis?
items.explanation: Complex formed visual hallucinations with preserved insight in a person with significant visual loss describe Charles Bonnet syndrome, thought to arise from cortical deafferentation. Dementia with Lewy bodies would produce fluctuating cognition and parkinsonism. Peduncular hallucinosis follows midbrain lesions, and late-onset schizophrenia would show delusions and loss of insight. Reassurance and treating the visual loss are the usual management.

items.stem: A 55-year-old woman who underwent a gastric bypass six years ago has a spastic gait and sensory ataxia. Her B12 is normal, and she has anemia and neutropenia. Which laboratory test will most likely clarify the diagnosis?
options: Serum very long chain fatty acids
items.explanation: Copper deficiency after bariatric surgery or with excess zinc ingestion produces a myeloneuropathy resembling B12 deficiency, with anemia and neutropenia. Low serum copper and ceruloplasmin confirm it, and replacement stops progression. Vitamin E deficiency produces ataxia with areflexia and malabsorption, though not cytopenias. Antinuclear antibodies and very long chain fatty acids do not fit the presentation.

items.stem: A 34-year-old man started on a dopamine antagonist for psychosis develops rigidity, fever of 40 degrees C, autonomic instability, altered consciousness, and a creatine kinase of 12,000 U/L. Which is the best acute management?
options: Continue the drug at a reduced dose with monitoring
Give cyproheptadine as the sole therapy
Start an anticholinergic agent as the only therapy
Stop the drug and give supportive care
items.explanation: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome produces rigidity, hyperthermia, and raised creatine kinase over days after dopamine blockade, which contrasts with serotonin syndrome, where clonus and a faster onset are expected. The offending drug is stopped, supportive care is given, and dantrolene or bromocriptine may be added. Continuing the drug is dangerous. Cyproheptadine and anticholinergics do not address the mechanism.

items.stem: A 38-year-old woman notes that loud noises make her dizzy and cause oscillopsia, and she hears her own eye movements. Computed tomography of the temporal bones shows a bony defect over the anterior semicircular canal. What is this disorder?
options: Perilymph fistula from a stapes prosthesis
items.explanation: Autophony, sound induced vertigo (the Tullio phenomenon), and a missing bony roof over the superior semicircular canal define superior canal dehiscence. The defect creates a third mobile window into the inner ear. There is no prior stapes surgery in this case to suggest a prosthesis fistula. Otosclerosis causes conductive hearing loss, and a schwannoma does not produce a bony defect.

items.stem: A 50-year-old man has progressive leg weakness, stepwise worsening with exertion, and flow voids along the dorsal surface of the thoracic cord on magnetic resonance imaging. Spinal angiography confirms the lesion. Which is the most common type?
items.explanation: A spinal dural arteriovenous fistula is the most common spinal vascular malformation, typically in middle-aged men, causing venous hypertension and a progressive myelopathy with dorsal serpentine flow voids. Cavernous malformations and telangiectasias do not produce flow voids in this pattern. A glioma enhances and expands the cord. Treatment is endovascular or surgical obliteration. Early treatment prevents irreversible myelopathy.

items.stem: A 41-year-old man has a seizure after an overdose of bupropion. His tachycardia is marked, and the electrocardiogram shows a widened QRS. Which drug is least appropriate for treating his seizure?
items.explanation: Drug-induced seizures from agents such as bupropion, tramadol, and tricyclic antidepressants are treated with benzodiazepines first and sometimes propofol, because they act on gamma-aminobutyric acid receptors. Sodium channel blockers such as phenytoin are ineffective and may add cardiac conduction toxicity in the setting of wide QRS toxicity. Lorazepam and midazolam are standard first choices. Sodium bicarbonate is added for the widened QRS interval.

items.stem: A 27-year-old woman taking a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor takes a large dose of tramadol and develops agitation, diaphoresis, clonus, hyperreflexia, and a temperature of 39.5 degrees C. Which agent can be used if supportive care is insufficient?
items.explanation: Serotonin syndrome is a clinical triad of mental status change, autonomic instability, and neuromuscular excitation with clonus and hyperreflexia, developing within hours. After stopping serotonergic drugs and giving benzodiazepines, cyproheptadine, a serotonin antagonist, may be added. Bromocriptine and dantrolene are used for neuroleptic malignant syndrome, and haloperidol can worsen the condition. Hyperthermia above 41 degrees C needs sedation, paralysis, and intubation.

items.stem: A 64-year-old man has subacute confusion and a periventricular, homogeneously enhancing lesion crossing the corpus callosum. The lesion enhances and shrinks after steroids, and cerebrospinal fluid cytology is pending. Which step is best before more steroids?
options: Broad-spectrum antibiotics only for empiric care
items.explanation: Primary central nervous system lymphoma classically appears as a homogeneously enhancing periventricular mass that can cross the corpus callosum, and steroids can cause lesions to disappear, making tissue diagnosis difficult. Stereotactic biopsy is preferred, and steroids are withheld if possible. Resection offers no survival benefit, and empirical radiation or antibiotics skip the diagnosis. High-dose methotrexate is the backbone of treatment once diagnosed.

items.stem: A 31-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes has a seizure after an insulin overdose. Her glucose is 20 mg/dL, and the seizure stops spontaneously. What is the most appropriate management?
items.explanation: Seizures in profound hypoglycemia are provoked events that resolve when glucose is restored, and chronic antiseizure therapy is not indicated. Treatment is intravenous dextrose with monitoring. Phenytoin is not required for an isolated metabolic seizure, intubation is reserved for airway compromise, and imaging delays the immediate reversible treatment. Persistent deficits after glucose normalization should prompt a search for another cause such as structural injury.

items.stem: A 70-year-old man is admitted after an overdose and has a respiratory rate of 6 per minute, pinpoint pupils, and coma. Which drug should be given first?
items.explanation: The triad of respiratory depression, miosis, and coma is classic for opioid toxicity, and naloxone is the specific competitive antagonist. Titrated dosing avoids precipitating severe withdrawal. Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines and can provoke seizures in dependent users, physostigmine treats anticholinergic toxicity, and atropine treats cholinergic excess with a different pupil and secretion pattern. Respiratory support is needed first when ventilation is inadequate, and repeat doses may be needed because naloxone is short-acting.

items.stem: A 33-year-old woman has amenorrhea, galactorrhea, and a serum prolactin of 180 ng/mL. Magnetic resonance imaging shows a 1.5-cm pituitary adenoma. What is first-line treatment?
options: A dopamine agonist such as cabergoline
items.explanation: Prolactinomas are the most common functioning pituitary adenomas, and dopamine agonists such as cabergoline normalize prolactin and shrink most tumors, so they are first-line even for macroadenomas. Surgery is used for resistance or intolerance. Radiation is a later option, and octreotide treats growth hormone secreting tumors. Visual fields and pituitary function should be checked, and treatment is often continued for years.

items.stem: A 38-year-old farmer develops salivation, lacrimation, diarrhea, miosis, bradycardia, and fasciculations after spraying a pesticide without protection. Which pair of drugs is appropriate?
items.explanation: Organophosphate poisoning inhibits acetylcholinesterase and produces a cholinergic crisis with muscarinic and nicotinic signs. Atropine reverses the muscarinic effects, and pralidoxime reactivates the enzyme if given before aging occurs. Neostigmine and physostigmine are cholinesterase inhibitors that worsen the crisis, and naloxone and flumazenil reverse opioid and benzodiazepine effects. Early treatment is critical, and decontamination of skin and clothing protects the staff.

items.stem: A 67-year-old woman has new jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, and sudden loss of vision in one eye. Her erythrocyte sedimentation rate is 90 mm per hour. What should be done before biopsy confirmation?
options: Wait for temporal artery biopsy results
Order outpatient ophthalmology review in two weeks
items.explanation: Giant cell arteritis with visual loss is an emergency, since the second eye can be lost within days. High-dose steroids are started at once, and the biopsy remains diagnostic for up to about two weeks after starting therapy. Waiting wastes the window to protect the other eye. Aspirin alone does not suppress the vasculitis, and a two-week delay is unacceptable.

items.stem: A 22-year-old woman reports a ten-minute loss of consciousness after a car accident. She has a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 14 at arrival, with a normal head computed tomography. How is the traumatic brain injury severity classified?
options: Moderate, as any loss of consciousness is moderate
Mild, as the score is 13 to 15
Cannot be classified without magnetic resonance imaging
items.explanation: Severity is graded by the Glasgow Coma Scale after resuscitation, with 13 to 15 mild, 9 to 12 moderate, and 8 or less severe. Loss of consciousness under 30 minutes with a normal examination and a score of 14 fits mild injury. Duration of unconsciousness and amnesia refine prognosis but do not change the category, and imaging is not required for grading.

items.stem: A 9-year-old boy has a headache for two months. He has papilledema, a left esotropia in primary gaze, and cannot abduct the left eye. Brain imaging shows a posterior fossa mass with hydrocephalus. What best explains the eye findings?
options: Direct invasion of the left oculomotor nerve by tumor
Internuclear ophthalmoplegia from a medial longitudinal lesion
False localizing sixth nerve palsy from raised pressure
A lesion of the left frontal eye field cortex
items.explanation: The abducens nerve has a long intracranial course and is stretched against the petrous ridge when pressure rises, so unilateral or bilateral sixth nerve palsy is a false localizing sign. The oculomotor nerve would cause ptosis and a down and out eye. Internuclear ophthalmoplegia impairs adduction. A frontal eye field lesion causes a gaze preference, not isolated abduction weakness.

items.stem: A 30-year-old woman has bilateral optic disc swelling, daily headache, and transient visual obscurations. Body mass index is 36, and magnetic resonance imaging and venography are normal. Lumbar puncture opening pressure is 35 cm of water with normal cerebrospinal fluid composition. What is the first-line medication?
items.explanation: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension is diagnosed by papilledema, normal imaging, normal cerebrospinal fluid, and elevated pressure. Weight loss and acetazolamide are first-line, as shown in the idiopathic intracranial hypertension treatment trial. Topiramate is an alternative option, not a replacement. Steroids can worsen weight gain, and furosemide alone is less effective than a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor. Regular visual field testing guides escalation to surgery.

items.stem: A 4-year-old child has morning vomiting, ataxia, and a midline cerebellar mass that enhances and causes obstructive hydrocephalus. Which tumor is most likely?
options: Pilocytic astrocytoma of the optic nerve
items.explanation: A midline posterior fossa mass in a young child with obstructive hydrocephalus and truncal ataxia is classically medulloblastoma, the most common malignant childhood brain tumor, which can disseminate through the cerebrospinal fluid. Meningioma and primary central nervous system lymphoma are tumors of adults, and an optic pathway glioma does not arise in the cerebellum. Treatment combines surgery, craniospinal radiation, and chemotherapy.

items.stem: An 82-year-old woman on a direct oral anticoagulant has a fall and then developing confusion and mild left hemiparesis over a week. Computed tomography shows a crescent-shaped hypodense collection with midline shift. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Continue anticoagulation and observe at home
items.explanation: A crescent-shaped collection crossing sutures with mass effect is a chronic subdural hematoma, common in older anticoagulated patients after minor trauma. Symptomatic hematomas with shift are drained by burr hole or craniotomy, and anticoagulation is reversed first. Observation alone risks herniation. Alteplase would worsen bleeding, and seizure surgery is irrelevant. Chronic subdural hematomas often follow minor trauma in older adults on antithrombotic drugs.

items.stem: A 32-year-old man in a high-speed collision is unconscious on arrival with a normal computed tomography scan except for small punctate hemorrhages at the gray-white junction. Magnetic resonance imaging later shows lesions in the corpus callosum. What is the diagnosis?
items.explanation: Prolonged unconsciousness after rotational acceleration with a relatively normal early scan and small hemorrhagic lesions at the gray-white junction, corpus callosum, and dorsolateral brainstem indicates diffuse axonal injury. An epidural hematoma is a visible extra-axial collection, venous thrombosis shows a dense sinus, and normal pressure hydrocephalus is a chronic gait and cognitive disorder. Prognosis relates to the depth and duration of coma.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman has three days of painful right eye movement and blurred vision. Visual acuity is 20/100 on the right, and a relative afferent pupillary defect is present. Fundus examination is normal. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
options: Oral prednisone at a low dose
items.explanation: Acute optic neuritis with painful eye movement and a normal disc is retrobulbar. High-dose intravenous methylprednisolone hastens visual recovery, although it does not change final acuity. Low-dose oral prednisone was linked to a higher recurrence rate in the optic neuritis trial. Immunoglobulin lacks supporting evidence in the acute setting, and simple observation withholds a therapy that speeds recovery.

items.stem: Eight months after a severe traumatic brain injury with a contusion, a 28-year-old man has a first focal seizure with impaired awareness. He has no other risk factors. Which statement about post-traumatic epilepsy is correct?
options: Prophylactic therapy prevents all late seizures
Late seizures occur only after penetrating injury
Prophylaxis reduces early but not late seizures
Risk is unrelated to injury severity
items.explanation: Early seizures within a week occur in a minority of severe injuries, and a short course of antiseizure medication reduces them, but it does not prevent late epilepsy. Risk rises with severity, cortical contusion, subdural hematoma, and penetrating injury, but closed injuries also carry risk. Late seizures after injury are treated as epilepsy, usually with long-term therapy.

items.stem: A 52-year-old woman has a right pupil that is 7 mm and poorly reactive to light with slow tonic constriction to near effort. Deep tendon reflexes are absent in both ankles. What is the likeliest cause of the pupil?
options: Compressive third nerve palsy from an aneurysm
Pharmacologic blockade from a topical anticholinergic
items.explanation: Light near dissociation with a tonic pupil and areflexia describes Adie syndrome, caused by damage to the ciliary ganglion or postganglionic fibers. The pupil constricts to dilute pilocarpine because of denervation supersensitivity. A third nerve aneurysm palsy would be accompanied by ptosis and ophthalmoplegia, and pharmacologic blockade does not respond to pilocarpine. Sympathetic interruption produces a small pupil.

items.stem: An elderly woman has a bitemporal hemianopia and fatigue. Magnetic resonance imaging shows a sellar mass compressing the chiasm from below. Which part of the visual field is lost first?
items.explanation: Inferior compression, as from a pituitary adenoma, hits the inferior crossing nasal retinal fibers first, so the superior temporal fields are lost first. Suprasellar masses such as craniopharyngioma compress from above and produce inferior temporal defects first. Nasal field loss would not result from chiasmal compression, and central scotomas suggest optic nerve disease. Perimetry therefore helps localize the mass before imaging confirms it.

items.stem: A 35-year-old woman has multiple schwannomas, bilateral vestibular schwannomas, and meningiomas. Which gene is affected?
items.explanation: Bilateral vestibular schwannomas are the hallmark of neurofibromatosis type 2, caused by mutations in the NF2 gene encoding merlin, and patients also develop meningiomas and ependymomas. NF1 causes neurofibromas, cafe au lait spots, and optic glioma. TSC1 causes tuberous sclerosis, and VHL causes hemangioblastomas and renal tumors. Patients need regular magnetic resonance imaging surveillance and hearing preservation planning, and bevacizumab may help schwannoma growth.

items.stem: A 49-year-old woman with end-stage kidney disease has asterixis, myoclonus, and confusion with a blood urea nitrogen of 120 mg/dL. Which management is most effective?
items.explanation: Uremic encephalopathy features asterixis, multifocal myoclonus, and altered mentation, and improves with dialysis, which removes the retained toxins. Levetiracetam accumulates in renal failure and can worsen sedation without addressing the cause. Pyridoxine and plasma exchange have no role in uremia. Levetiracetam and other renally cleared drugs accumulate and need dose adjustment. Symptoms usually improve within days of effective dialysis. Pyridoxine is used for isoniazid toxicity, not for uremic confusion.

items.stem: A 41-year-old woman with a history of migraine has spontaneous attacks of vertigo lasting from minutes to several hours, sometimes with headache and photophobia. Audiometry and imaging are normal. Which diagnosis best fits?
items.explanation: Recurrent spontaneous or positional vertigo lasting five minutes to 72 hours in a patient with migraine, with migraine features during at least some attacks and no better explanation, defines vestibular migraine. Meniere disease requires documented hearing loss. A schwannoma shows progressive unilateral hearing loss and an enhancing mass, and superior canal dehiscence produces sound or pressure induced vertigo.

items.stem: A 62-year-old man has sudden painless loss of vision in the left eye on waking. The disc is swollen with a few flame hemorrhages, and the fellow disc is small with a cup-to-disc ratio near zero. Which diagnosis is most likely?
items.explanation: A crowded disc at risk in the fellow eye and painless sudden loss with segmental disc edema are typical of nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy. The arteritic form occurs in older patients with systemic symptoms, a high sedimentation rate, and often a pale swollen disc. Venous occlusion shows diffuse retinal hemorrhages. Leber disease affects young men subacutely and sequentially.

items.stem: A 25-year-old man has diplopia that worsens at the end of the day, with variable ptosis improving after a minute of upgaze and an ice pack test that improves ptosis. Pupils are normal. Which antibody test is most appropriate?
items.explanation: Fatigable ptosis and diplopia with normal pupils, with improvement after cooling, indicate ocular myasthenia gravis. About half of purely ocular cases have acetylcholine receptor antibodies. Calcium channel antibodies indicate Lambert-Eaton syndrome, aquaporin-4 antibody indicates neuromyelitis optica, and anti-GQ1b antibody is linked to Miller Fisher syndrome, which causes areflexia and ataxia. Antibody negative cases may need single fiber or repetitive stimulation studies.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman has recurrent episodes of vertigo lasting about two hours, with left ear fullness, fluctuating low frequency hearing loss, and roaring tinnitus. Between attacks she is well. Which dietary measure is a reasonable first step?
options: Fluid loading of three liters daily
items.explanation: The syndrome of episodic vertigo lasting minutes to hours with fluctuating low frequency hearing loss, tinnitus, and aural fullness is Meniere disease, attributed to endolymphatic hydrops. A low-sodium diet, with diuretics if needed, is the usual initial therapy. Large fluid loading has no supporting evidence. Protein intake and potassium supplementation do not influence endolymphatic pressure.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman has headache and sudden visual loss with ophthalmoplegia, hypotension, and altered consciousness. Imaging shows hemorrhage into a pituitary macroadenoma. What is the immediate priority?
options: Dopamine agonist titration over several weeks
Observation alone without steroids or surgery
items.explanation: Pituitary apoplexy results from hemorrhage or infarction into an adenoma and can cause acute adrenal insufficiency along with chiasmal and cavernous sinus compression. Immediate glucocorticoid replacement is life-saving, and decompression is considered when vision or consciousness deteriorates. A dopamine agonist alone is too slow, and radiation is not an emergency measure. Cortisol deficiency is the main cause of death, so replacement should not wait for laboratory confirmation.

items.stem: A 20-year-old football player has headache, dizziness, and difficulty concentrating after a helmet collision, with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15, a normal neurologic examination, and no loss of consciousness. What is the best advice?
options: Strict dark-room rest without any activity for several weeks
Immediate return to play if symptoms ease within ten minutes
Routine computed tomography and hospital admission for observation
Brief relative rest, then gradual stepwise return
items.explanation: Concussion is a clinical diagnosis, and imaging is unnecessary without red flags. Current consensus favors one or two days of relative rest, then gradual symptom limited activity, with return to play only after symptoms resolve and a graded protocol is passed. Prolonged strict rest delays recovery. Same-day return risks second impact complications. Symptoms usually resolve within about two weeks in most adults.

items.stem: A 38-year-old man has a seizure, and magnetic resonance imaging shows a nonenhancing left frontal mass. Pathology shows an astrocytoma with an IDH1 mutation and loss of ATRX expression. Which diagnosis is correct under current classification?
items.explanation: In the current classification, diffuse gliomas in adults are separated by molecular markers. An IDH-mutant tumor with ATRX loss and TP53 mutation is an astrocytoma, whereas 1p/19q codeletion with IDH mutation defines an oligodendroglioma. IDH-wildtype diffuse tumors with specific molecular features are glioblastoma, and pilocytic astrocytoma is a circumscribed childhood tumor. IDH mutation also confers a better prognosis than wildtype tumors.

items.stem: A 25-year-old man is struck on the side of the head, loses consciousness briefly, wakes, and then declines over two hours into coma. Computed tomography shows a biconvex hyperdense lesion. Which vessel is most likely injured?
items.explanation: A lucid interval after a temporal bone fracture and a lens-shaped hyperdense collection that does not cross suture lines indicate an epidural hematoma, usually from middle meningeal artery laceration. Subdural hematomas arise from bridging veins and appear crescentic. The anterior cerebral artery and sagittal sinus are less common sources and give different patterns. Prompt surgical evacuation gives an excellent outcome when done early.

items.stem: A 68-year-old man with aortic surgery has sudden bilateral leg weakness and loss of pain and temperature sensation below the umbilicus. Vibration and position sense are preserved, and bladder function is lost. Which vessel territory is involved?
items.explanation: Spinal cord infarction produces sudden onset paraparesis with loss of spinothalamic modalities and sphincter control while dorsal column function is spared, which matches the anterior spinal artery territory. The posterior spinal arteries supply the dorsal columns. Vertebral artery disease causes brainstem signs, and the sagittal sinus is a cerebral venous structure. Aortic surgery and dissection are common causes, and outcome is often poor.

items.stem: A 64-year-old woman with a serum sodium of 108 mEq/L from a thiazide diuretic has a seizure. After a hypertonic saline bolus, what is the maximum safe rise in sodium over the first 24 hours?
items.explanation: Chronic hyponatremia corrected too rapidly risks osmotic demyelination, so correction is limited to about 8 mEq/L per day in patients at high risk and to no more than 10 to 12 in others. Brain cells adapt to chronic hyponatremia by losing osmolytes and cannot quickly regain them. Rises of 15 or more in a day carry a high risk of pontine and extrapontine injury.

items.stem: A 55-year-old woman has a droopy right eyelid and double vision developing over two days with a severe right-sided headache. The right pupil is 6 mm and unreactive, and the eye is down and out. What is the most urgent next step?
options: Outpatient lumbar puncture in one week
Reassurance because diabetes is the usual cause
items.explanation: A third nerve palsy with a dilated unreactive pupil indicates external compression of the superficial pupillomotor fibers, most often by a posterior communicating artery aneurysm, and needs emergent angiography. Ischemic diabetic palsies typically spare the pupil. Edrophonium addresses myasthenia, which does not affect the pupil. Delayed lumbar puncture risks aneurysm rupture. Delay risks rupture and permanent third nerve damage.

items.stem: A 34-year-old man has a cape-like loss of pain and temperature sensation over the shoulders and arms, hand muscle atrophy, and preserved vibration sense. Magnetic resonance imaging of the cervical cord shows a longitudinal cavity. Which associated finding is most likely?
items.explanation: Syringomyelia produces a suspended dissociated sensory loss because the cavity interrupts crossing spinothalamic fibers while sparing dorsal columns, with lower motor neuron weakness in the hands. Most cases are linked to a Chiari I malformation with altered cerebrospinal fluid flow at the foramen magnum. The other lesions have no direct relationship to syrinx formation. Decompression of the foramen magnum may stabilize the syrinx.

items.stem: A 58-year-old man with a glioma on chronic high-dose dexamethasone for edema develops proximal leg weakness with normal creatine kinase and normal reflexes. What is the likely cause?
items.explanation: Painless proximal weakness during prolonged glucocorticoid use with a normal creatine kinase and electromyography showing little abnormality is characteristic of steroid myopathy, which improves on dose reduction. Polymyositis raises creatine kinase, and Lambert-Eaton syndrome features reduced reflexes and autonomic signs. Guillain-Barre syndrome causes areflexia and an ascending pattern. Switching to a nonfluorinated steroid and exercise may help.

items.stem: A 61-year-old man with small cell lung cancer has subacute limb-girdle weakness, dry mouth, and areflexia that improves with repeated contraction. Which antibody is expected?
items.explanation: Proximal weakness with autonomic features and reflexes that improve after exercise, in a patient with small cell lung cancer, is Lambert-Eaton syndrome, caused by antibodies to presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels. Acetylcholine receptor antibodies cause myasthenia gravis. Anti-Hu antibodies cause sensory neuronopathy and encephalomyelitis, and anti-NMDA receptor antibodies cause encephalitis. Chest imaging should look for a small cell lung cancer, and 3,4-diaminopyridine improves strength.

items.stem: A 57-year-old woman with a long history of poor diet presents with confusion, a wide-based gait, and horizontal gaze-evoked nystagmus with bilateral abducens weakness. What should be given first?
items.explanation: The triad of encephalopathy, ataxia, and ocular signs defines Wernicke encephalopathy, a thiamine deficiency state seen in malnutrition, hyperemesis, and bariatric surgery. Thiamine is given parenterally before or with glucose to avoid precipitating or worsening the syndrome. Glucose alone can consume remaining thiamine. Folate and steroids do not treat the deficiency. Delay risks progression to Korsakoff syndrome with permanent memory loss.

items.stem: A 36-year-old motorcyclist has a flaccid, areflexic paralysis of the legs after a thoracic fracture. Twelve hours later she is hypotensive with a heart rate of 48. What explains the vital signs?
options: Hypovolemic shock from occult bleeding in the abdomen
Autonomic dysreflexia from a bladder trigger
items.explanation: Injury above about T6 interrupts descending sympathetic pathways, causing hypotension with bradycardia, unlike hypovolemic shock, which causes tachycardia. Management includes fluids and vasopressors to maintain mean arterial pressure. Autonomic dysreflexia causes severe hypertension with a noxious stimulus below the lesion, and cardiogenic shock would not explain the bradycardia pattern. Atropine can be used for symptomatic bradycardia, and hypovolemia from bleeding should still be excluded in trauma.

items.stem: A 58-year-old man with cirrhosis has day-night sleep reversal, asterixis, and a fluctuating confusion after a gastrointestinal bleed. Which treatment is first-line for overt episodes?
items.explanation: Overt hepatic encephalopathy is treated by correcting precipitants and giving lactulose, which acidifies the colon and traps ammonia, with rifaximin added to prevent recurrence. Benzodiazepines can precipitate or worsen encephalopathy. Prolonged protein restriction worsens malnutrition and is no longer recommended. Antipsychotics alone do not treat the cause. Rifaximin is added to lactulose to reduce the risk of recurrence, and precipitants such as bleeding, infection, or electrolyte shifts are corrected.

items.stem: A 58-year-old man has acute continuous vertigo and vomiting for six hours. He cannot walk unaided. Examination shows direction-changing gaze-evoked nystagmus, a normal head impulse test bilaterally, and no hearing loss. Which interpretation is correct?
options: Findings favor a central cause such as cerebellar stroke
Findings indicate posterior canal benign positional vertigo
items.explanation: In acute vestibular syndrome, a normal head impulse test, direction-changing nystagmus, or skew deviation points to a central lesion, since a peripheral lesion produces an abnormal head impulse on the affected side. Vestibular neuritis shows unidirectional nystagmus and an abnormal head impulse. Meniere disease is episodic with hearing loss, and benign positional vertigo is brief and triggered by position.

items.stem: A 61-year-old woman with a malignancy has constipation, polyuria, confusion, and a corrected serum calcium of 14.2 mg/dL. After intravenous fluids, which medication provides the most durable control?
items.explanation: Hypercalcemia of malignancy causes confusion, polyuria, and constipation. After volume repletion, bisphosphonates such as zoledronic acid inhibit osteoclastic bone resorption and give lasting control. Loop diuretics are used only for volume overload. Dietary calcium restriction has little effect on malignant hypercalcemia, and thiazides raise serum calcium and are contraindicated. Calcitonin acts quickly but briefly, and denosumab is used when bisphosphonates fail.

items.stem: A 47-year-old woman with breast cancer has headaches, diplopia, and a cauda equina syndrome. Magnetic resonance imaging shows linear enhancement along the cerebellar folia and nerve roots. Which test has the greatest diagnostic yield?
options: Cerebrospinal fluid cytology, repeated if negative
Brain biopsy as the first test
items.explanation: Leptomeningeal metastasis presents with multifocal cranial nerve and spinal root deficits and linear leptomeningeal enhancement. Cerebrospinal fluid cytology confirms the diagnosis, with sensitivity rising from about half after a single sample to higher after repeated large volume samples. Electroencephalography and nerve conduction studies are not diagnostic, and biopsy is rarely required. Cerebrospinal fluid protein is typically raised and glucose lowered.

items.stem: A 54-year-old woman completed whole brain radiation two years ago. She now has progressive memory decline, gait apraxia, and urinary incontinence with ventriculomegaly. Which complication is most likely?
options: Tumor progression is the only possibility
items.explanation: Late radiation injury appears months to years after treatment, causing cognitive decline, gait disturbance, and incontinence, and may mimic normal pressure hydrocephalus. Acute encephalopathy occurs during treatment with edema, and the early delayed somnolence syndrome appears weeks after treatment and resolves. Progression is possible but is not the only explanation of this pattern. Shunt surgery is of uncertain benefit in this setting.

items.stem: A 65-year-old woman has gradual cognitive slowing, a flapping tremor, and profound fatigue. Serum sodium is 118 mEq/L, serum osmolality is low, urine osmolality is high, and she appears euvolemic. What is the likeliest mechanism?
items.explanation: Hypotonic hyponatremia with inappropriately concentrated urine and euvolemia is the signature of the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion, often due to drugs, lung malignancy, or central nervous system disease. Cerebral salt wasting involves volume depletion. Primary polydipsia gives dilute urine, and hypovolemia would produce clinical signs of fluid loss and low urinary sodium. Fluid restriction is the usual first step.

items.stem: A 60-year-old woman has a newly diagnosed IDH-wildtype glioblastoma, resected maximally. She is in good functional status. Which standard adjuvant regimen is recommended?
options: Radiation with concurrent and adjuvant temozolomide
items.explanation: The standard of care for newly diagnosed glioblastoma in a fit patient is maximal safe resection followed by focal radiation with concurrent temozolomide and then adjuvant temozolomide. Methylation of the MGMT promoter predicts benefit from alkylating chemotherapy. Whole brain radiation alone and observation are inferior, and methotrexate treats primary central nervous system lymphoma. Tumor treating fields may be added to maintenance therapy in selected patients.

items.stem: A 62-year-old man with prostate cancer has back pain, then leg weakness over two days, with a thoracic sensory level. Magnetic resonance imaging confirms epidural cord compression. What should be started immediately?
options: Oral analgesics with outpatient review in a week
Systemic chemotherapy alone as first treatment
Physical therapy for strengthening and gait training
items.explanation: Malignant epidural spinal cord compression is an oncologic emergency, and early steroids reduce edema while radiation or decompressive surgery preserves function, since pretreatment function strongly predicts outcome. Waiting for outpatient review allows permanent paralysis. Chemotherapy alone is too slow except in highly sensitive tumors, and physical therapy does not treat compression. Prognosis for walking depends strongly on the function present when treatment begins.

items.stem: A 33-year-old woman has episodic vertigo lasting seconds whenever she rolls onto her right side in bed. The Dix-Hallpike maneuver to the right triggers upbeat torsional nystagmus lasting 20 seconds with a short latency. Which treatment is most appropriate?
items.explanation: Brief positional vertigo with a latent, fatiguing torsional upbeating nystagmus is posterior canal benign paroxysmal positional vertigo. The Epley canalith repositioning maneuver is first line and often curative in one session. Vestibular suppressants delay central compensation and do not treat the cause. Corticosteroids help vestibular neuritis, and intratympanic gentamicin is reserved for refractory Meniere disease.

items.stem: A 48-year-old woman with Graves disease has proptosis, lid retraction, and horizontal diplopia. Magnetic resonance imaging shows enlargement of extraocular muscle bellies with sparing of the tendons. Which muscle is most commonly involved first?
items.explanation: Thyroid eye disease causes inflammation and fibrosis of the muscle bellies with tendon sparing, which separates it from orbital myositis. The inferior rectus is affected most often, followed by the medial rectus, producing restricted upgaze. The lateral rectus and superior oblique are involved less often. Euthyroid status does not exclude the disorder. Smoking and radioiodine can worsen the course, and euthyroid disease occurs.

items.stem: Three weeks after carbon monoxide poisoning from which she recovered, a 45-year-old woman develops apathy, memory loss, and parkinsonism. Magnetic resonance imaging is most likely to show which finding?
items.explanation: Delayed neurologic sequelae can appear days to weeks after apparent recovery from carbon monoxide poisoning, with cognitive and behavioral change and parkinsonism. The globus pallidus is selectively vulnerable and shows T2 hyperintensity, along with leukoencephalopathy. Occipital infarcts and cerebellar atrophy do not characterize this syndrome, and an abscess would produce fever and focal signs. Hyperbaric oxygen may reduce the risk of these sequelae in selected patients.

items.stem: A 19-year-old man has tremor, dysarthria, and behavioral change, with golden-brown rings at the corneal limbus. Serum ceruloplasmin is low. Which treatment is appropriate for the long term?
options: Chelation with penicillamine or trientine, or zinc
items.explanation: Wilson disease causes copper accumulation in the liver and basal ganglia, with Kayser-Fleischer rings and low ceruloplasmin. Lifelong chelation, or zinc to block intestinal absorption, removes or limits copper. Copper supplements would worsen the disease. Levodopa alone does not address the cause of the movement disorder, and plasma exchange is reserved for acute liver failure situations.

items.stem: A 60-year-old man sees constant bilateral shimmering static across his whole visual field, with afterimages and trailing, for years. Examination and imaging are normal. Which diagnosis fits best?
items.explanation: Continuous tiny flickering dots across the visual field, with palinopsia and normal examination, define visual snow syndrome, which often coexists with migraine and tinnitus. Occipital seizures are brief and stereotyped, and retinal detachment gives a curtain-like field loss. Optic neuritis causes reduced acuity and an afferent pupillary defect. Treatment is difficult, and no consistently effective drug exists, so reassurance matters.

items.stem: A 56-year-old woman receiving a platinum-based chemotherapy regimen develops numbness and loss of vibration and joint position in a stocking-glove pattern with early hearing loss. Which neuropathy type is most likely?
options: A pure motor axonal neuropathy of the distal limbs
A demyelinating motor neuropathy with conduction block
A neuromuscular junction disorder with fatigable weakness
items.explanation: Cisplatin and related platinum agents injure the dorsal root ganglion, producing a large fiber sensory neuronopathy with ototoxicity, in a dose related pattern. Motor neuropathy is not prominent. Vincristine causes a mixed axonal neuropathy with distal weakness and autonomic features, and a junction disorder would produce fatigable weakness and not progressive sensory ataxia. Ototoxicity and neuropathy limit the cumulative dose of the drug.

items.stem: A 55-year-old woman has progressive hand clumsiness, gait instability, hyperreflexia, a positive Hoffmann sign, and neck stiffness. Magnetic resonance imaging shows cord compression at C5 to C6 with T2 signal change. What is the best management?
options: Physical therapy only for twelve months
items.explanation: Degenerative cervical myelopathy with upper motor neuron signs, hand dysfunction, and cord signal change is progressive, and surgical decompression is recommended for moderate to severe disease or progression. Steroids do not treat chronic compression. Conservative care alone is reserved for mild stable disease, and lumbar puncture is unnecessary and may be risky in the setting of a tight canal.

items.stem: A 52-year-old woman has a headache, and imaging shows a dural-based, homogeneously enhancing extra-axial mass with a dural tail over the convexity. She has no symptoms otherwise. What is the best management?
options: Observation with serial imaging if small and asymptomatic
items.explanation: A dural-based enhancing mass with a dural tail is most consistent with meningioma, the most common benign primary intracranial tumor. Small asymptomatic lesions are observed with serial imaging, with surgery or radiosurgery for growth or symptoms. Chemotherapy and whole brain radiation have no role, and steroids are used only for symptomatic edema. Higher grade or symptomatic lesions are treated with surgery and radiation.

items.stem: A 36-year-old woman has anisocoria that is greater in the dark than in the light. The larger pupil constricts briskly to light, and the smaller right pupil shows ptosis and mild anhidrosis of the face. Which agent confirms the localization best?
items.explanation: Horner syndrome leaves the sympathetically denervated pupil unable to dilate in dim light. Apraclonidine, a weak alpha agonist, dilates the denervated pupil because of receptor supersensitivity, which reverses the anisocoria. Dilute pilocarpine is used to test for an Adie tonic pupil. Tropicamide dilates any pupil and cannot separate causes, and physostigmine only constricts the pupil.

items.stem: A 6-year-old girl has a lumbosacral hairy patch, a bladder that does not empty well, and progressive foot deformity with leg weakness. Magnetic resonance imaging shows the conus at the L4 level with a thickened filum. What is the best treatment?
items.explanation: A low-lying conus, a thickened filum, cutaneous markers, and progressive neurogenic bladder and orthopedic changes indicate tethered cord syndrome, which is treated by surgical release to prevent further deficits. Watching without surgery risks irreversible damage. Steroids do not release the tether, and an intrathecal baclofen pump manages spasticity rather than the cause. Early release improves bladder and motor outcomes.

items.stem: A 4-year-old child living in an old house with peeling paint has irritability, abdominal pain, constipation, and developmental regression. Radiographs show dense bands at the long bone metaphyses. What treatment is indicated if the blood lead level is very high?
options: Chelation therapy, together with source removal
items.explanation: Lead poisoning in children causes cognitive decline, abdominal pain, anemia, and radiodense metaphyseal lines. Source removal is essential, and chelating agents such as succimer or dimercaprol with calcium disodium edetate are used above defined thresholds, with encephalopathy requiring urgent combined therapy. Plasma exchange does not clear tissue bound lead, and iron or B12 alone do not treat the toxicity.

items.stem: Four days after rapid correction of severe hyponatremia, a 52-year-old man becomes dysarthric and quadriparetic with pseudobulbar signs and later becomes locked in. Which imaging finding is expected?
options: T2 hyperintensity in the central pons
items.explanation: A biphasic course of initial improvement followed by quadriparesis, pseudobulbar palsy, and locked-in syndrome after rapid correction points to central pontine myelinolysis. Imaging shows a symmetric central pontine T2 lesion, sometimes with extrapontine changes. Medial thalamic infarcts cause somnolence and gaze palsy, and hippocampal or cortical changes suggest limbic encephalitis or prion disease. Prevention by slow correction matters because no specific therapy reverses the lesion.

items.stem: A 3-month-old infant has a flattened posterior fossa, headache-equivalent irritability, and later develops stridor and dysphagia. Magnetic resonance imaging shows the cerebellar tonsils and brainstem herniated through the foramen magnum along with a myelomeningocele. Which malformation is it?
items.explanation: Chiari II malformation is associated with myelomeningocele and involves herniation of the cerebellar vermis and brainstem with hydrocephalus, often presenting with stridor and dysphagia from brainstem dysfunction. Chiari I involves only tonsillar descent and usually presents in adulthood. Dandy-Walker malformation shows cystic enlargement of the fourth ventricle without herniation, and an arachnoid cyst does not herniate.

items.stem: A 35-year-old man has episodes of sudden profound leg weakness on waking after a high-carbohydrate meal. He also has palpitations and tremor, and his serum potassium is 2.4 mEq/L during an attack. Which underlying disorder should be tested for?
items.explanation: Thyrotoxic periodic paralysis causes hypokalemic attacks triggered by carbohydrate loads or rest after exercise, mostly in men of Asian descent, and resolves once the hyperthyroid state is treated. Adrenal insufficiency causes hyperkalemia. Hypothyroidism does not cause hypokalemic paralysis, and the pituitary does not directly produce aldosterone. Beta blockers can reduce adrenergic symptoms and attacks while euthyroid status is restored, and potassium repletion should be cautious to avoid rebound hyperkalemia.

items.stem: A 45-year-old man falls on his outstretched hands and has weakness greater in the arms than the legs, with burning dysesthesias of the hands and variable sensory loss. Radiographs show no fracture and he has cervical stenosis. Which syndrome is this?
items.explanation: Hyperextension injury in a patient with cervical spondylosis damages the central gray matter and medial corticospinal fibers, where arm fibers lie, so the arms are weaker than the legs with variable sensory loss. Anterior cord syndrome spares dorsal columns, Brown-Sequard shows ipsilateral motor and contralateral pain loss, and posterior cord syndrome causes proprioceptive loss. Recovery is usually best in the legs and bladder.
